title: VII. And In The Open Air
paragraphs: “The air out here is fresh, but in my apartment it isn’t, not in any sense of the word. Let’s take it slowly, sir. I’d be glad of your kind interest.”
“There’s something important I want to tell you too,” said Alyosha. “I just don’t know how to start.”

“Naturally you have business with me. You’d never have dropped in on me without a reason. Unless you came only to complain about the boy, and that’s hardly likely. And speaking of the boy, I couldn’t explain in there, but out here I’ll tell you how that scene went. A week ago my tow was thicker—I mean my beard. That’s the nickname they have for my beard, the schoolboys most of all. Well, your brother Dmitri Fyodorovitch had me by the beard and was pulling. I’d done nothing. He was in a towering rage and I just happened to cross his path. He dragged me out of the tavern into the market-place, and right then the boys were coming out of school, Ilusha among them. The moment he saw me in that state, he ran to me. ‘Father,’ he cried, ‘father!’ He grabbed me, hugged me, tried to pull me free, and shouted at the man who was attacking me, ‘Let go, let go, it’s my father, forgive him!’—yes, he really did cry ‘forgive him.’ He seized that hand, that very hand, in his little hands and kissed it.... I remember his little face at that moment. I haven’t forgotten it and I never will!”

“I swear,” cried Alyosha, “my brother will tell you how deeply and sincerely he regrets it, even if he has to get down on his knees in that same market-place.... I’ll make him, or he’s no brother of mine!”

“Aha, so it’s only an idea of yours! It doesn’t come from him at all, just from the generosity of your own warm heart. You should have said so. Well, in that case let me tell you about your brother’s highly chivalrous, soldierly generosity, because he did show some at the time. He stopped dragging me by the beard and let me go. ‘You’re an officer,’ he said, ‘and I’m an officer. If you can find a decent man to act as your second, send me your challenge. I’ll give you satisfaction, even though you’re a scoundrel.’ That’s what he said. A chivalrous spirit indeed! I went off with Ilusha, and that scene is now a family record, printed forever on Ilusha’s soul. No, noblemen’s privileges are not for the likes of us. Judge for yourself. You’ve just been in our mansion. What did you see? Three ladies. One is a cripple and weak in the head, another is a cripple and a hunchback, and the third isn’t crippled but is far too clever. She’s a student, dying to get back to Petersburg and work for the emancipation of the Russian woman on the banks of the Neva. I won’t mention Ilusha; he’s only nine. I’m alone in the world, and if I die, what becomes of them all? That’s all I ask you. And suppose I challenge him and he kills me on the spot. Then what? What becomes of them? Or worse, suppose he doesn’t kill me but only maims me. I couldn’t work, yet I’d still be a mouth to feed. Who would feed me, and who would feed them all? Should I take Ilusha out of school and send him begging in the streets? That’s what it means for me to challenge him to a duel. It’s silly talk, nothing more.”
“He will beg your forgiveness. He will bow down at your feet in the middle of the market-place,” cried Alyosha again, his eyes glowing.

“I did think of taking him to court,” the captain went on, “but look in our legal code. Could I get much compensation for a personal injury? And then Agrafena Alexandrovna[3] sent for me and screamed at me, ‘Don’t even dream of it! If you go after him, I’ll announce to the whole world that he beat you because you were dishonest, and then you’ll be the one prosecuted.’ I call God to witness whose dishonesty it was, and on whose orders I acted. Wasn’t it on her own and Fyodor Pavlovitch’s? ‘And what’s more,’ she went on, ‘I’ll dismiss you for good, and you’ll never earn another penny from me. I’ll talk to my merchant too’ (that’s what she calls her old man) ‘and he’ll dismiss you!’ And if he dismisses me, who else will pay me anything? Those two are all I have to look to. Your Fyodor Pavlovitch has not only stopped giving me work, for a different reason, but he means to use some papers I signed to sue me. So I kept quiet, and you’ve seen what our retreat looks like. But now let me ask you something. Did Ilusha hurt your finger badly? I didn’t like to bring it up in our mansion, with him there.”

“Yes, badly, and he was in a great fury. He was avenging you on me, as a Karamazov. I see that now. But if only you’d seen how he was hurling stones at his schoolmates! It’s very dangerous. They could kill him. They’re children, and stupid. A stone gets thrown and somebody’s head is broken.”
“That’s just what has happened. A stone hit him today. Not on the head but on the chest, right over the heart. He came home crying and groaning, and now he’s ill.”
“And you know, he goes after them first. He holds a grudge against them on your account. They say he stuck a penknife into a boy named Krassotkin not long ago.”
“I’ve heard about that too. It’s dangerous. Krassotkin is an official here, so we may hear more about it.”
“I’d advise you,” Alyosha went on warmly, “not to send him to school at all for a while, until he’s calmer ... and his anger has passed.”

“Anger!” the captain repeated. “That’s exactly what it is. He’s a little creature, but it’s a mighty anger. You don’t know the whole of it, sir. Let me tell you more. Ever since that day all the boys have been teasing him about the ‘wisp of tow.’ Schoolboys are a merciless race. One at a time they’re angels, but together, and especially at school, they’re often merciless. Their teasing roused a gallant spirit in Ilusha. An ordinary boy, a weak son, would have given in and felt ashamed of his father, sir. He stood up for his father against all of them. For his father, and for truth and justice. What he suffered when he kissed your brother’s hand and cried to him ‘Forgive father, forgive him’—only God knows that, and I, his father. Because our children—not your children, but ours, the children of poor gentlemen that everybody looks down on—know what justice means, sir, even at nine years old. How should the rich know? They never go down into such depths in their whole lives. But in the square, at the moment he kissed that hand, my Ilusha understood all that justice means. That truth went into him and crushed him for good, sir,” the captain said hotly again, in a sort of frenzy, striking his right fist against his left palm as if to show how “the truth” had crushed Ilusha. “That same day, sir, he came down with a fever and was delirious all night. All day he hardly said a word to me, but I noticed he kept watching me from his corner, though he turned to the window and pretended to be studying his lessons. I could see his mind wasn’t on them. The next day I got drunk to forget my troubles, sinful man that I am, and I don’t remember much. Mamma started crying too—I’m very fond of mamma—well, I spent my last penny drowning my troubles. Don’t despise me for it, sir. In Russia the men who drink are the best. The best men among us are the biggest drunkards. I lay down, and I remember nothing about Ilusha, though all that day the boys were jeering at him at school. ‘Wisp of tow!’ they shouted. ‘Your father got dragged out of the tavern by his wisp of tow, and you ran along and begged forgiveness.’”

“On the third day, when he came back from school, I saw he looked pale and miserable. ‘What is it?’ I asked. He wouldn’t answer. Well, there’s no talking in our mansion without mamma and the girls joining in. Besides, the girls had heard about it on the very first day. Varvara had started snarling: ‘You fools and buffoons, can you ever do anything sensible?’ ‘Quite so,’ I said, ‘can we ever do anything sensible?’ That was how I turned it aside for the moment. So in the evening I took the boy out for a walk. You should know that we walk every evening, always the same way, the way we’re going now, from our gate to that big stone lying by itself in the road under the hurdle, where the town pasture begins. A beautiful, lonely spot, sir. Ilusha and I walked along hand in hand as usual. He has a little hand, his fingers are thin and cold—he suffers with his chest, you know. ‘Father,’ he said, ‘father!’ ‘Well?’ said I. I saw his eyes flashing. ‘Father, the way he treated you!’ ‘It can’t be helped, Ilusha,’ I said. ‘Don’t forgive him, father, don’t forgive him! At school they say he paid you ten roubles for it.’ ‘No, Ilusha,’ said I, ‘I wouldn’t take money from him for anything.’ Then he started trembling all over, took my hand in both of his and kissed it again. ‘Father,’ he said, ‘father, challenge him to a duel. At school they say you’re a coward and won’t challenge him, and that you’ll take ten roubles from him.’ ‘I can’t challenge him to a duel, Ilusha,’ I answered. And I told him in a few words what I’ve just told you. He listened. ‘Father,’ he said, ‘all the same, don’t forgive it. When I’m grown up I’ll call him out myself and kill him.’ His eyes shone and blazed. And of course I’m his father, so I had to put in a word. ‘It’s a sin to kill,’ I said, ‘even in a duel.’ ‘Father,’ he said, ‘when I’m grown up I’ll knock him down, knock the sword out of his hand, fall on him, wave my sword over him and say: “I could kill you, but I forgive you, so there!”’ You see what his little mind has been working on these two days. He must have been planning that revenge all day long, and raving about it at night.

“But then he started coming home from school badly beaten. I found out about it the day before yesterday, and you’re right, I won’t send him to that school any more. I heard that he was standing up to the whole class on his own and defying them all, that his heart was full of resentment and bitterness. I was frightened for him. We went for another walk. ‘Father,’ he asked, ‘are the rich stronger than anybody else on earth?’ ‘Yes, Ilusha,’ I said, ‘nobody on earth is stronger than the rich.’ ‘Father,’ he said, ‘I’ll get rich, I’ll become an officer and conquer everybody. The Tsar will reward me, I’ll come back here, and then no one will dare—’ Then he fell silent, though his lips kept trembling. ‘Father,’ he said, ‘what a horrid town this is.’ ‘Yes, Ilusha,’ I said, ‘it’s not a very nice town.’ ‘Father, let’s move to another town, a nice one,’ he said, ‘where people don’t know about us.’ ‘We’ll move, we will, Ilusha,’ said I, ‘only I have to save up first.’ I was glad I could turn his mind from painful thoughts, and we started dreaming about how we’d move to another town, and how we’d buy a horse and cart. ‘We’ll put mamma and your sisters inside, cover them up, and we’ll go on foot. You’ll get a ride now and then, and I’ll walk beside you, because we have to look after our horse. We can’t all ride. That’s how we’ll travel.’ He was delighted, most of all by the idea of having a horse and driving it. Of course, a Russian boy is born among horses. We chattered for a long time. Thank God, I thought, I’ve distracted him and comforted him.

“That was the day before yesterday, in the evening, but last night everything changed. He’d gone to school in the morning and came home low, terribly low. In the evening I took him by the hand and we went for our walk, but he wouldn’t talk. A wind was blowing, there was no sun, it felt like autumn, and twilight was coming on. We walked along, both of us low in spirits. ‘Well, my boy,’ said I, ‘what about setting off on our travels?’ I thought I might lead him back to our talk of the day before. He didn’t answer, but I felt his fingers trembling in my hand. Ah, I thought, this is bad; something new has happened. We’d reached the stone where we are now. I sat down on the stone. And in the sky there were lots of kites flapping and spinning. As many as thirty were in sight. Of course, it’s just the season for kites. ‘Look, Ilusha,’ said I, ‘it’s time we got out last year’s kite again. I’ll mend it. Where did you put it away?’ My boy made no answer. He looked off to one side and turned away from me. And then a gust of wind blew up the sand. He suddenly fell on me, threw both his little arms around my neck and held on tight. You know how it is with children who are silent and proud and fight back their tears in great trouble: when they finally break down, the tears come in streams. With those warm streams of tears he suddenly wet my face. He sobbed and shook as if in convulsions, and pressed himself against me where I sat on the stone. ‘Father,’ he kept crying, ‘dear father, how he insulted you!’ And I sobbed too. We sat there shaking in each other’s arms. ‘Ilusha,’ I said to him, ‘Ilusha darling.’ No one saw us then. God alone saw us. I hope He will count it in my favor. You must thank your brother, Alexey Fyodorovitch. No, sir, I will not thrash my boy to please you.”

The captain had slid back into his old tone of bitter clowning. Still, Alyosha sensed that the man trusted him. Had anyone else been standing there in Alyosha’s place, he thought, the captain would never have spoken so openly or told what he had just told. That gave Alyosha courage, though his heart was close to tears.
“Oh, I would so love to be friends with your boy!” he cried. “If you could arrange it—”
“Of course, sir,” the captain muttered.

“But now hear something quite different!” Alyosha went on. “I have a message for you. My brother Dmitri has wronged his fiancée too. She is a noble-hearted girl, and you have probably heard of her. I have every right to tell you how she was wronged. In fact I ought to, because the moment she heard of the insult to you, and of your unfortunate situation, she sent me to bring you this help. That was just now. It comes from her alone. It does not come from Dmitri, who has abandoned her, or from me, his brother, or from anyone else. It is from her, only from her! She begs you to accept it.... The same man has insulted you both. She thought of you just after he had done something similar to her, similar in its cruelty, I mean. She comes as a sister to help a brother in trouble.... She told me to persuade you to take these two hundred roubles from her, as from a sister, because she knows how badly you need them. Nobody will know about it, and no one can start any unjust gossip. Here are the two hundred roubles. I swear you must take them, unless—unless all men on earth are meant to be enemies! But there are brothers even on earth.... Your heart is generous ... you must see that, you must,” and Alyosha held out two new hundred-rouble notes, the rainbow-colored kind.

The two of them stood by the great stone near the fence, and nobody was close by. The notes seemed to hit the captain with tremendous force. He started, but at first only out of astonishment. He had never imagined their talk would end like this. Help from anyone was the furthest thing from his dreams, let alone a sum like that!
He took the notes. For a minute he could hardly answer, and a completely new look came over his face.
“That’s for me? All that money, two hundred roubles! Good heavens! Why, I haven’t laid eyes on so much money for four years! Mercy on us! And she says she’s a sister.... Is that really true?”
“I swear that all I’ve told you is true,” cried Alyosha.
The captain went red in the face.

“Listen, my dear, listen. If I take it, I’m not behaving like a scoundrel? To you, Alexey Fyodorovitch, I won’t seem a scoundrel? No, Alexey Fyodorovitch, listen, listen,” he hurried on, plucking at Alyosha with both hands. “You’re talking me into taking it, saying it comes from a sister, but deep down in your heart, won’t you despise me if I take it, eh?”
“No, no! I swear on my salvation I won’t! And nobody will ever know except me, you, her, and one other lady, her great friend.”

“Forget the lady! Listen, Alexey Fyodorovitch, at a moment like this you have to listen, because you can’t understand what these two hundred roubles mean to me now.” The poor man was working himself up, little by little, into a rambling, almost wild excitement. He had lost his balance, and he talked very fast, as if afraid he would be cut off before he could say everything.

“Besides its being honestly come by, from a ‘sister’ I respect and revere so highly, do you know, I can now look after mamma and Nina, my hunchback angel of a daughter? Doctor Herzenstube came to see us, out of the goodness of his heart, and spent a whole hour examining the two of them. ‘I can’t make anything of it,’ he said. But he prescribed a mineral water, sold at the chemist’s here. He said it would surely do her good, and he ordered baths as well, with some medicine in the water. The mineral water costs thirty kopecks a bottle, and she might need forty of them. So I took the prescription, put it on the shelf under the ikons, and there it lies. And for Nina he ordered hot baths, with something dissolved in them, morning and evening. But how are we to manage a cure like that in our mansion? We have no servants, no help, no bath, not even any water! Nina has rheumatism all over, I don’t think I mentioned that. At night her whole right side aches. She’s in agony, and would you believe it, the angel suffers without a groan, so as not to wake us. We eat whatever we can find, and she will take only the scraps, what you’d hardly throw to a dog. ‘I don’t deserve it, I’m taking it from you, I’m a burden to you,’ that’s what her angel eyes are trying to say. We wait on her, but she hates it. ‘I’m a useless cripple, good for nothing.’ As if she didn’t deserve it, when she is what saves all of us, with her angelic sweetness! Without her, without her gentle word, it would be hell among us! She softens even Varvara. And don’t judge Varvara harshly either. She’s an angel too, and she’s been wronged too. She came to us for the summer with sixteen roubles she had saved from giving lessons, meant for her trip back to Petersburg in September, which is now. But we took her money and lived on it, so now she has nothing to go back with. Not that she could go back anyway, since she has to slave for us here. She’s like an overworked horse with all of us riding on her back. She waits on everyone, mends, washes, sweeps the floor, puts mamma to bed. And mamma is capricious and tearful and out of her mind! But now, with this money, I can hire a servant, you understand, Alexey Fyodorovitch. I can buy medicines for the dear creatures. I can send my student to Petersburg. I can buy beef and feed them properly. Good Lord, it’s a dream!”
Alyosha was overjoyed that he had given the man such happiness, and that the poor fellow had let himself be made happy.

“Wait, Alexey Fyodorovitch, wait,” the captain broke in, talking with frenzied speed, swept off by a fresh daydream. “Do you know, Ilusha and I may actually carry out our dream. We’ll buy a horse and cart, a black horse, he insists on black, and we’ll set off just as we pretended the other day. I have an old friend, a lawyer in K. province. A man I trust told me that if I came, this friend would give me a place as a clerk in his office. Who knows, maybe he would! So I’d simply put mamma and Nina in the cart, Ilusha would drive, and I’d walk, I’d walk.... Why, if I could just collect one debt that’s owed me, I might even have enough for that!”

“You would have enough!” cried Alyosha. “Katerina Ivanovna will send you as much more as you need. And I have money too, you know. Take what you want, as from a brother, from a friend, and pay it back later.... (You’ll get rich, you’ll get rich!) And you couldn’t have a better idea than moving to another province! It would save you, and especially your boy. You ought to go soon, before winter, before the cold sets in. Write to us when you get there, and we will always be brothers.... No, it’s not a dream!”

Alyosha was so happy he could have hugged him. But he glanced at the man and stopped short. The captain stood with his neck stretched out and his lips thrust forward, his face pale and frenzied. His lips kept moving, as if he were trying to get something out. No sound came, yet they went on moving. It was eerie.
“What is it?” asked Alyosha, startled.

“Alexey Fyodorovitch ... I ... you,” the captain muttered, stumbling, staring at him with a strange, wild, fixed gaze and a look of desperate resolve. At the same time something like a grin played on his lips. “I ... you, sir ... would you like me to show you a little trick I know?” he murmured suddenly, in a firm, quick whisper, his voice no longer stumbling.
“What trick?”
“A pretty one,” the captain whispered. His mouth was twisted to the left, and his left eye was squeezed shut. He kept staring at Alyosha.
“What’s the matter? What trick?” cried Alyosha, now truly alarmed.

“Why, look!” the captain suddenly squealed. All through the conversation he had been holding the two notes by one corner between thumb and forefinger. Now he showed them to Alyosha, then crushed them savagely into a ball in his right fist. “Do you see? Do you see?” he shrieked, white and furious. And suddenly he flung up his hand and hurled the crumpled notes onto the sand. “Do you see?” he shrieked again, pointing at them. “Look at that!”
And in a wild rage he started stamping on them with his heel, panting and shouting as he did it:
“There’s your money for you! There’s your money for you! There’s your money for you! There’s your money for you!”
Then he leaped back and drew himself up in front of Alyosha, and his whole figure spoke of unspeakable pride.

“Tell the people who sent you that the wisp of tow does not sell his honor,” he cried, raising his arm in the air. Then he whirled around and began to run. But he had not gone five steps when he turned all the way back and blew a kiss to Alyosha. He ran five paces more and turned for the last time. This time his face was not twisted with laughter. It was quivering with tears. In a tearful, broken, sobbing voice he cried:
“What could I say to my boy if I took money from you to pay for our shame?”

And then he ran on without looking back. Alyosha watched him go, grieved beyond words. Oh, he saw that until the very last moment the man had not known he would crush the notes and throw them away. The captain did not turn back, and Alyosha knew he would not. He would not follow or call him back, and he knew why. When the man was out of sight, Alyosha picked up the two notes. They were badly crumpled and had been ground into the sand, but they were not torn. They even rustled like new ones when Alyosha unfolded and smoothed them out. Once he had smoothed them, he folded them, put them in his pocket, and went to Katerina Ivanovna to report on the success of her errand.
